Given this current positioning, we believe it is more suitable for us to operate as an open, community-driven open-source project. We do not need aggressive promotion or PR outreach. Instead, organic discovery fits our stage and community atmosphere best.

We can casually share relevant links to our solutions and code resources during discussions (such as in Magician threads). All links will point to our official organization repositories. Since we have already prepared clear guidance in the repository README, community members can naturally learn about our work and participate on their own.

This low-key, organic discovery approach is the most appropriate and standard growth path for our open-source project at this stage.

I think we can follow the same low-key and community-first direction for all of our public introduction materials.

All public content can be written mainly to attract and invite more developers to join the ecosystem, keeping a similar encouraging and resonant tone as our current organization profile. Instead of highlighting individual work, the content should focus on empowering the whole community — helping everyone share their technical ideas, ERC-related research, and designs, and pushing forward open and collective ecosystem building together.

I also understand that contributors hope to get proper credit and recognition for their work. I think this can be well balanced by properly managing project admin and review permissions.

The community will naturally recognize the core maintainers over time, through ongoing PR reviews, code maintenance, and daily community governance work. There is no need for excessive formal emphasis, as long-term collaboration will make the project’s operating structure clear to everyone ✨🤝

Not exploitable by an outside attacker today (the pinned issuer signs the full preimage, so it can't be forged), but his fix is right regardless: pre-compute the content-field offset off-chain, have the contract verify the marker sits at that exact index rather than scanning for it. He also flagged a real gas optimization in BIP340.sol (pre-compute the sqrt off-chain, verify ry^2==y2 mod p on-chain instead of a modexp call every time). Both worth fixing before anything closer to mainnet - good, credible review, not a formality.

For me recompute-don't-trust is the floor — fully with you, it's the thing that makes any of it real. But when I ask "toward what," my answer comes from the seam I keep standing in: composition.

Each piece is one leg of the same animal — identity, task, input-provenance, the anchor, verification, eligibility, settlement, reputation. On their own they're good ERCs.
Wired together they're the first stack where an autonomous agent can actually run a real job end to end: say who it is, prove what it did, show the work is genuine, get paid, and carry that into its reputation — with no trusted party at any join. I don't think that whole thing exists anywhere else yet.

So if I had to name the direction: a trustless agent economy you can execute, not just describe. Recompute is what keeps each seam honest; composition is what turns the seams into something an agent can actually live on. onchain-ai growing its own structure feels like the same instinct one level up — the reference impls need a home that itself composes.

And it grabbed me for a non-academic reason. dinamic.eth has been my own run at exactly this composability from day one, honestly more a lab than a business, something I started on my own and keep bending as I learn. Everything I pick up in this group I've been folding straight back into it, and the things it actually needed, a rescue that had to be provable to strangers, an escrow that couldn't be allowed to trust its own operator, kept turning out to be a standard that was already here, or one gap away. The recompute-kit already verifies records for agents and CI (primitives, MCP, recipes, the tri-state verdict: verified-good 0 / verified-bad 1 / unverifiable 2). What it lacks is a human surface. Add one and it becomes a human-provable system: a person points at a record + its source, the kit recomputes, and the person sees the reproduction happen, step by step, ending in the tri-state verdict.

The distinction that matters: verifiability vs legibility
Two different trust models, usually conflated:

Verifiability (zkML) Legibility (recompute)
What you get a succinct proof a program checks a reproduction a human reads
To a human it is a black box — trust the circuit, the setup, the proof system transparent — you watch it rebuild from inputs
Reveals the artifact? no (its strength — privacy) yes (its strength — auditability)
Cost / availability heavy; impractical for full LLMs today cheap; works now
Answers “was this (possibly secret) computation valid?” “is this record honest + reproducible from its sources?”
For most off-chain records — receipts, decisions, agent runs, documents — the real dispute is the second question, and it wants legibility. When the primary artifact can be shown, hiding it behind a proof is a downgrade in trust: you’ve traded “see it yourself” for “trust my circuit.”

They’re complementary, not competing: zkML when the artifact must stay secret; recompute when it can be inspected. “zkML is the ultimate answer to everything” is the tell that someone’s selling the hammer, not solving the problem — it’s an excellent hammer for a specific nail (succinct + private verification), over-generalized to every trust problem.

Engine: the existing recompute-kit (recompute-step recipes, the commitment/receipt/onchain primitives, the tri-state verdict).
Surface (new): a UI where a human supplies (record, primary source, pinned ref) → the kit runs the matching recipe → shows the reproduction inline (the derivation, the intermediate hashes, the comparison) → renders the tri-state verdict with a plain-language reason.
Key UX principle: never just a green checkmark — always the reproduction. The verdict is the by-product; the legible rebuild is the product. That’s what a checkmark you must trust can’t give.
Reuses the verdict vocabulary already locked in the eligibility↔verdict correspondence note (admit/reject/undetermined ↔ verified-good/bad/unverifiable); unverifiable shown honestly as “couldn’t evaluate,” never dressed as pass.
